screens.title: Your cat is part of a food chain
lines: When your cat pounces on a sparrow in the backyard, she's the top of a food chain you can watch from the window.
That sparrow ate caterpillars, the caterpillars ate the rosebush, and the rosebush ate sunlight. Energy is on the move.

vocab.meaning: a living thing that makes its own food from sunlight, like a plant
a living thing that gets energy by eating other living things
a path showing who eats whom, with energy passing along it

screens.framing: No grade, no pressure — just explore. Even a guess teaches your brain what to notice.

screens.title: Waves carry energy, not stuff
lines: Pluck a tight strand of knitting yarn and it shivers — but the yarn itself stays put. The wiggle (the energy) travels; the yarn doesn't go anywhere.
Feel a K-pop bass drop in your chest: that thump is a sound wave moving energy through the air to you, while the air just jiggles in place.

vocab.meaning: a disturbance that carries energy from place to place without carrying the material along
how many wave cycles pass a point each second
how big a wave's swing is — its height from the middle line

screens.framing: No grade here — just try it. Wrong guesses still tune your instincts.

screens.title: Thinking like a scientist (and a baker)
lines: Every time you tweak a cookie recipe and ask 'did that make them chewier?', you're running an experiment.
Scientists just make it FAIR and write down the evidence — then argue from it. Let's learn the moves.

vocab.meaning: anything in an experiment that can change, like oven temperature or amount of sugar
a test where you change only ONE thing and keep everything else the same
a claim is your answer, evidence is the data behind it, reasoning explains why the data supports the claim

items.prompt: Backyard food chain: rosebush → caterpillar → sparrow → your cat. No grade here — just explore: which one is the PRODUCER that makes its own food?
items.hint: Producers don't eat anything — they capture sunlight.
items.explanation: The rosebush is the producer: it makes food from sunlight. Everything after it is a consumer that eats to get energy.

items.prompt: Let's follow the energy through that backyard food chain together.

steps.text: It starts with the SUN. The rosebush is a producer: it captures sunlight and stores that energy as food (sugar). In a food chain, arrows point the way energy FLOWS.
The caterpillar is a consumer — it can't make food, so it eats the rosebush's leaves to get that stored energy. We draw rosebush → caterpillar, the arrow pointing TO the eater.

check.question: Why does the arrow point toward the caterpillar, not away from it?
options: Because energy flows INTO the thing that eats
Because caterpillars are bigger than leaves

steps.text: The sparrow eats the caterpillar, and your cat eats the sparrow. Each arrow passes energy up the chain: caterpillar → sparrow → cat.
But here's the twist: only about a tenth of the energy makes it to each next level — the rest is used up living and moving. That's why food chains stay short.

check.question: Why are there usually only 4–5 links in a food chain?
options: Energy shrinks at every step, so little is left near the top
The sun runs out of light

steps.text: So energy flows one way: sun → rosebush → caterpillar → sparrow → cat, shrinking each step. Your cat rules the top on the leftovers. 🐱

items.prompt: Your turn — finish tracing this pond food chain: algae → minnow → heron.

lines: Algae is the producer: it makes its own food from [[sunlight]].
The minnow eats the algae, so the energy arrow points to the [[minnow]].
Energy flows one way: algae → minnow → [[heron]].

items.hint: Producers capture light; arrows point toward whatever does the eating.
items.explanation: Energy starts in the producer (algae) and flows up the chain: algae → minnow → heron.

items.prompt: Your cat naps in a backyard full of living and non-living things. Which of these is an ABIOTIC (non-living) part of that ecosystem?
items.hint: Abiotic parts were never alive.
items.explanation: Abiotic means non-living — rocks, water, air, sunlight. The worm, dandelion, and sparrow are all biotic (living).

items.prompt: Sort each part of a pond into living or non-living.
items.hint: If it can grow, eat, or reproduce, it's biotic.
items.explanation: Biotic = living (frog, reed, beetle); abiotic = the non-living surroundings (water, sunlight, mud).

items.prompt: Fill in the three roles every ecosystem needs.

lines: A [[producer]] makes its own food from sunlight.
A [[consumer]] gets energy by eating other living things.
A [[decomposer]] breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil.

items.hint: Think: the maker, the eater, the recycler.
items.explanation: Producers make food, consumers eat, and decomposers recycle the leftovers back into the soil.

items.prompt: Grass is a producer. What does it use to make its own food?
items.hint: Producers run on light, not on eating.
items.explanation: Through photosynthesis, producers turn sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar — their food.

items.prompt: Which biome is hot and dry, with cacti and animals that hide from the midday heat?
items.hint: Think of a place with very little rain and lots of sand.
items.explanation: A desert is defined by very low rainfall; its plants and animals are built to save water.

items.prompt: In the Herbology greenhouse, drag each organism into its ecosystem role.
items.hint: Producers make food, consumers eat it, decomposers break down the dead.
items.explanation: The plants (mandrake, geranium) produce; the gnome and flobberworm consume; the fungus and bacteria decompose.

items.prompt: How is a food WEB different from a single food chain?
items.answer: A food web links many food chains, since most animals eat several things and are eaten by several others
options: A food web links many food chains, since most animals eat several things and are eaten by several others
A food web contains only plants
A food web shows energy flowing in a never-ending circle
A food web is just a food chain drawn backwards
items.hint: Real animals rarely eat just one food.
items.explanation: A food web is many overlapping food chains, because organisms usually have several food sources and predators.

items.prompt: Label this meadow food web. Energy starts at the sun.
items.hint: Find the energy source, the plant, the plant-eater, the meat-eater, and the recycler.
items.explanation: Sun → clover (producer) → grasshopper (herbivore) → shrew (carnivore); the mushroom (decomposer) recycles the dead.

items.prompt: Put this ocean food chain in order, starting with the producer.
items.hint: Producers come first; the largest predator is last.
items.explanation: Energy flows phytoplankton → krill → mackerel → seal.

items.prompt: Air is almost four-fifths nitrogen, but plants can't grab it from the sky. What changes nitrogen into a form plant roots can absorb?
items.answer: Bacteria in the soil and on plant roots
options: Bacteria in the soil and on plant roots
Rain washing it off the leaves
items.hint: Tiny living recyclers underground do this job.
items.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn air nitrogen into compounds plants can take up through their roots.

items.prompt: Label this grassland energy pyramid, widest level first.
items.hint: The bottom level makes its own food; energy shrinks going up.
items.explanation: Producers (grasses) hold the most energy; it passes up to grasshopper → lizard → hawk, shrinking about 90% each step.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about energy pyramids are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes up to the next level.
The producer level at the bottom has the most available energy.
data.lie: Top predators have the most energy available to them.

items.explanation: Energy shrinks about 90% at every step, so the top level has the LEAST energy — which is why top predators are rare.

items.prompt: Label this enchanted-forest food web.
items.hint: Trace energy from the sun to the producer, then up to the predators.
items.explanation: Sun → oak (producer) → deer (herbivore) → wolf (carnivore); the toadstool (decomposer) breaks down the dead.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about decomposers are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals.
Decomposers return nutrients to the soil so producers can use them again.
data.lie: A healthy ecosystem doesn't really need decomposers.

items.explanation: Without decomposers, dead matter and nutrients would pile up and never cycle back, and producers would starve — decomposers are essential.

items.prompt: Match each population interaction to an example.

pairs: A cat stalking and catching a mouse
Two oak trees reaching for the same sunlight
A bee feeding on nectar while pollinating a flower
A mushroom breaking down a fallen log

items.hint: Who hunts? Who shares a resource? Who BOTH benefit? Who recycles?
items.explanation: Predation = one hunts another; competition = both need the same resource; mutualism = both benefit; decomposition = breaking down the dead.

items.prompt: Trace water as it cycles through the environment.

lines: The sun heats a lake and water rises as vapor: [[evaporation]].
High up, the vapor cools into cloud droplets: [[condensation]].
The droplets fall back as rain or snow: [[precipitation]].

items.hint: Up as vapor, cool into clouds, fall back down.
items.explanation: Water cycles endlessly: evaporation → condensation → precipitation.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about the carbon cycle are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: A plant builds most of its body from carbon it pulls out of the air as carbon dioxide.
Breathing out (respiration) and decay return carbon to the air as carbon dioxide.
data.lie: Carbon gets used up and disappears as it passes through living things.

items.explanation: Carbon is never destroyed — it cycles: plants capture CO₂, animals eat plants, and respiration and decay release it again.

items.prompt: An energy pyramid starts with 60,000 kcal of energy in the producers. Using the 10% rule, how many kcal reach the SECONDARY consumers (two levels up)?
items.hint: Take 10%, then 10% of that.
items.explanation: 10% of 60,000 = 6,000 at the primary level, and 10% of 6,000 = 600 kcal at the secondary level.

items.prompt: In the wizarding forest's food chain the producers store 10,000 kcal. Using the 10% rule, how many kcal reach the TERTIARY consumers (three levels up)?
items.hint: Drop to a tenth, three times.
items.explanation: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kcal: about 90% is lost at every step, so the top predator gets very little.

items.prompt: A savanna easily feeds thousands of grass-eating zebras but only a few lions. Using the idea that about 90% of energy is lost at each step up a food chain, why?
items.answer: Each level up has far less energy, so the top can support only a few large predators
options: Each level up has far less energy, so the top can support only a few large predators
Zebras reproduce but lions never do
items.hint: Follow the shrinking energy from grass upward.
items.explanation: Only about 10% of energy passes up each step, so by the predator level there is little left — only a few top predators can be fed.

items.prompt: Legendary: an eagle is a tertiary consumer that needs 75 kcal of energy. Using the 10% rule (each level holds about ten times the level above it), at LEAST how many kcal must the producers capture from the sun?
items.hint: Work downward: multiply by 10 for each step from eagle back to the producers — three steps.
items.explanation: Eagle 75 → secondary 750 → primary 7,500 → producers 75,000 kcal. Energy loss means producers must capture far more than the top needs.
